title: Follow-ups from backend-data-provider-timeouts's PR #360 review
description: Non-blocking findings from pr-reviewer's PR #360 review of backend-data-provider-timeouts (needs_work verdict on that PR for a separate, blocking fail-fast-delay bug in GET /api/stocks/{ticker}/analysis's new concurrent fetch -- tracked as a review comment on the parent task itself, not here, since it must be fixed before that PR can merge). These four items are real but non-blocking: worth tracking so they aren't lost once the parent PR merges, per CLAUDE.md's 'every non-blocking finding becomes a tracked task' rule.

checklist.step: get_extended_data's own three property fetches (.calendar/.info/.insider_transactions) remain sequential; each is capped at 10s by the new _clamp_session_timeout, but the call as a whole can still take up to ~30s in the worst case -- the same 'sequential calls stacking' mechanism the parent task's own incident report describes, just moved one level down from get_analysis and only partially addressed by this PR's per-call timeout cap. Consider fetching these three concurrently too (mirroring the get_analysis-level fix, once its own fail-fast-delay bug is fixed) to bound get_extended_data's own worst case to roughly one timeout budget.

The new TestConcurrentFetch integration test (tests/integration/test_stocks_analysis.py) asserts elapsed wall-clock time is under 2x a 0.3s sleep -- confirmed genuinely discriminating (fails when reverted to sequential), but a wall-clock timing threshold like this carries some flakiness risk under heavy CI/sandbox scheduling load. Consider a more deterministic mechanism if this test is ever observed to flake (e.g. instrumenting call start/end order or overlap directly instead of timing it).

This PR's GET /api/stocks/{ticker}/analysis concurrent fetch is now the 4th near-identical hand-rolled 'with ThreadPoolExecutor(...) as executor: submit(...); .result()' block in the backend (app/portfolio/pricing.py, app/api/day_trader_signal.py, get_indicator_history in app/api/routers/stocks.py, and now get_analysis), with no shared helper factored out. Worth factoring into one shared utility -- especially relevant since the parent PR's blocking fail-fast-delay bug (ThreadPoolExecutor.__exit__'s shutdown(wait=True) delaying an early exception until every submitted future finishes) would need the same fix applied consistently across all of these call sites if any of them share the same bug shape.

backend/app/data/yfinance_provider.py sits at 97% line / 96% branch coverage after this PR: _clamp_session_timeout's inner re-check-after-acquiring-the-lock branch (line 73) and its defensive `except Exception: pass` around the attribute assignment (lines 91-92) are not exercised by any test -- both are genuinely best-effort/defensive paths (the first is hard to hit deterministically without instrumenting the lock; the second needs a session object that allows reading .request but rejects arbitrary attribute assignment). Worth a test if a clean way to trigger these is found, but low priority given both are intentionally never-raise safety nets.

From PR #360's third review round (round-2 fix's own PR comment): get_analysis's new get_data_provider_factory gives each of its 3 concurrent legs its own SessionLocal()-backed Session/connection, on top of the request's own Depends(get_db) session -- up to 4x this endpoint's prior per-request DB connection footprint, against an unsized QueuePool (pool_size=5/max_overflow=10 = 15 total, backend/app/db/session.py). Empirically tested at 10-12 concurrent requests (30-36 simultaneous connection demands vs the 15 cap): degrades gracefully today (connections queue, requests still complete, no OperationalError/pool TimeoutError observed) rather than failing outright, and a same-cache-row write race between legs is already handled by _upsert/_upsert_extended's pre-existing IntegrityError/OperationalError swallowing (PR #231). Worth reconsidering if this per-call-session pattern spreads to more endpoints, or if real usage ever approaches the concurrency levels where the pool's default 30s checkout timeout could actually be hit -- e.g. explicit pool sizing tied to how many concurrent per-leg sessions the app's endpoints can realistically open at once, or a lighter-weight per-leg resource than a full second Session.

decisions.decision: Made get_extended_data's three property fetches (.calendar/.info/.insider_transactions) concurrent via a manually-managed ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) with explicit shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True) in a finally block -- the same fail-fast shape app.api.routers.stocks.get_analysis already uses for its own daily/weekly/extended-data fetch -- rather than the with ThreadPoolExecutor(...) as executor: form.
decisions.rationale: Bounds get_extended_data's own worst case to roughly one _REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS budget instead of up to three stacking sequentially, closing the same 'sequential calls stacking' mechanism the parent task's incident report describes, one level down from get_analysis. Rejected the context-manager form (with ThreadPoolExecutor(...) as executor:) for the same reason PR #360's first review round rejected it at the get_analysis call site: its __exit__ unconditionally calls shutdown(wait=True), which would delay a fast failure (e.g. an immediate rate-limit/timeout on .calendar) by however long the slower of .info/.insider_transactions takes -- confirmed via a new mutation-tested regression test (TestGetExtendedData.test_fast_calendar_failure_returns_promptly_despite_slow_other_properties in tests/unit/data/test_yfinance_provider.py): reverting to the context-manager form makes it fail (elapsed climbs to ~1.0s instead of staying under 0.5s), confirming the fix is necessary and the test is discriminating. Deliberately did NOT reuse get_analysis's own per-leg-scoped-DataProvider/Session pattern (app.api.dependencies.get_data_provider_factory / _fetch_via_scoped_provider): that pattern exists specifically because get_analysis's abandoned legs each own a Session the request's own get_db teardown could otherwise race against (PR #360's second review round). Nothing in get_extended_data owns a DB Session at all -- it only reads yfinance Ticker properties against the process-wide YfData session singleton, which is never closed per-call -- so an abandoned property fetch left running in the background after shutdown(wait=False) simply finishes (or times out) on its own with nothing else depending on that timing; there is no race to close against. Also deliberately did not add Future.add_done_callback-based abandoned-leg-failure logging (unlike get_analysis's _log_if_abandoned_leg_failed): a discarded property-fetch failure here is no worse than this same code's own pre-existing behavior before concurrency was introduced (a sequential call that had already failed on an earlier property never even attempted the later ones, and the only caller-visible effect either way is that get_extended_data's own exception -- whichever leg's -- surfaces as a DataProviderUnavailableError; the fetch that would have succeeded is optional metadata, not required for the request to complete). Verified concurrency directly via a new deterministic (non-flaky) test, TestGetExtendedData.test_calendar_info_and_insider_transactions_are_fetched_concurrently, which records each property fetch's own (start, end) timestamps and asserts pairwise overlap rather than an aggregate elapsed-time threshold -- mutation-tested against reverting to the prior sequential code (confirmed fails: 'calendar and info did not overlap'). Full backend suite (1491 passed, 100% coverage on yfinance_provider.py specifically, 100% overall), ruff, and mypy all re-run clean; backend/openapi.json regenerated with zero diff (no route/schema touched).

decisions.decision: Hardened TestConcurrentFetch.test_daily_weekly_and_extended_data_are_fetched_concurrently (tests/integration/test_stocks_analysis.py) by adding a companion test, test_daily_weekly_and_extended_data_actually_overlap, that records each of get_analysis's three legs' own (start, end) wall-clock intervals (via a new call_intervals dict on _SlowStubProvider) and asserts every pair overlaps -- rather than replacing the existing aggregate-elapsed-time-threshold test outright.
decisions.rationale: The followups item's own concern was specifically the aggregate-threshold style (elapsed < sleep_seconds * 2): a single total-duration number can only prove 'the whole request took less time than sequential would', which is a slightly indirect proxy for 'the three fetches actually overlapped in time' -- a general slowdown of the whole test process (CI/sandbox scheduling jitter) inflates every leg's own duration roughly equally, so a pairwise-overlap check derived from each leg's own directly-recorded start/end timestamps is robust to that in a way an aggregate multiplier isn't, without needing to guess a bigger-but-still-arbitrary tolerance factor. Kept the original test rather than deleting it: it's still valid, still passes, and still directly demonstrates the practical latency-reduction outcome (bounded to roughly one timeout budget, not three) that this task's own incident report cares about -- the overlap test proves the mechanism (concurrency), the elapsed-time test proves the outcome (bounded latency); together they're strictly more informative than either alone, and CLAUDE.md's testing standard doesn't ask for redundant coverage to be pruned. Mutation-tested the new overlap test against a hand-reverted sequential get_analysis (three separate `with provider_factory() as p: ...` blocks instead of the concurrent ThreadPoolExecutor): confirmed it fails ('daily and weekly did not overlap'), same mutation-testing bar the original test was already held to. Applied the identical overlap-based hardening technique to the new get_extended_data-level concurrency tests in yfinance_provider.py's own test file (see the decision above), for consistency. Full backend suite re-run clean (1491 passed, 100% coverage).

decisions.decision: Deferred factoring pricing.py's enrich_positions_with_price, day_trader_signal.py's _fan_out_per_ticker, stocks.py's get_indicator_history, and stocks.py's get_analysis into one shared ThreadPoolExecutor-fan-out helper -- left all four as-is, no code change.
decisions.rationale: Re-read all four call sites (this task's own checklist item cites them) before deciding: enrich_positions_with_price and _fan_out_per_ticker share one genuinely-common shape (fan a fixed, known-in-advance collection of items out across a bounded thread pool, always fully wait via `with ThreadPoolExecutor(...) as executor:` before returning, collect every result) and could plausibly share a helper -- but get_indicator_history's own two-future daily+weekly fetch (also a full-wait `with` block, but exactly two named legs resolved by position rather than N homogeneous items resolved by key) and get_analysis's three-future fetch (fail-fast, manual shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True), per-leg-scoped DataProvider/Session, abandoned-leg logging) are both structurally different enough from that shape and from each other that a single shared helper covering all four would need either a lowest-common-denominator interface that loses get_analysis's fail-fast/scoped-session semantics (the actual bug PR #360 spent three review rounds fixing) and get_indicator_history's positional two-leg shape, or enough optional parameters/branches to approximate a small framework -- more risk of reintroducing a subtle regression in an already-hardened call site than the duplication it would remove is worth, for a followups task whose own instructions explicitly permit deferring exactly this kind of consolidation with a documented decision when it 'feels too invasive for a followups task'. A narrower, lower-risk version (unifying only enrich_positions_with_price and _fan_out_per_ticker, which do share the same shape) was considered and also deferred: their return shapes already differ deliberately (a List preserving input order for enrich_positions_with_price, per its own docstring's 'no per-ticker de-duplication needed' contrast with _fan_out_per_ticker's de-duplicating dict-keyed-by-ticker shape) for reasons specific to each caller, so even this narrower unification would need a shared low-level fan-out primitive parameterized over both dict-keyed and order-preserving output -- doable, but not the specific 'sequential calls stacking' latency/robustness problem this followups task and its parent both exist to fix, and not called out as blocking by PR #360's review. No code changed for this item; left as a standing observation, not lost, since a next reader of this task will see this same reasoning rather than having to re-derive it.

decisions.decision: Reconfirmed (no code change) that get_analysis's up-to-4x-per-request DB connection-pool footprint (backend/app/db/session.py's unsized QueuePool, pool_size=5/max_overflow=10) remains an acceptable, non-blocking risk.
decisions.rationale: backend/app/db/session.py is unchanged since PR #360's third review round's own empirical load test (10-12 concurrent requests, 30-36 simultaneous connection demands against the 15-connection cap, graceful queuing with no OperationalError/pool TimeoutError) and pr-decision's independent re-verification of the same result -- there is no new code on this path for this followups task to re-test against, and this task's own instructions explicitly say to 'only act on this if there's a concrete, low-risk improvement, otherwise it's fine to just confirm/reconfirm via a decisions entry and leave as-is.' Considered two concrete low-risk improvements and rejected both for this pass: (1) explicit pool_size/max_overflow sizing on the engine -- rejected because there's no evidence-based number to pick yet (this is a single-user/local app in every environment that's actually exercised it; an arbitrary larger number is not obviously safer than the SQLAlchemy default, and an arbitrary smaller number risks making the theoretical exhaustion scenario easier to hit, not harder); (2) a lighter-weight per-leg resource than a full second Session for get_data_provider_factory's per-leg scope -- rejected because CachedDataProvider's read-through-cache contract (app/data/cache.py) is written against a SQLAlchemy Session specifically (ORM upserts, IntegrityError/OperationalError swallowing), and inventing a narrower resource just for this one call site would duplicate that contract's logic rather than reuse it, for a risk this task's own findings already show degrades gracefully. Worth revisiting if either the per-call-session pattern spreads to more endpoints or real usage approaches the concurrency levels where the pool's default 30s checkout timeout could actually be hit -- neither has happened since PR #360 merged.

comments.summary: Nested ThreadPoolExecutor thread fan-out: get_analysis's own extended-data leg now calls into get_extended_data, which this PR made concurrent in its own right (a second, nested ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3)). One GET /api/stocks/{ticker}/analysis request can now transiently spin up up to 6 worker threads (3 outer + 3 inner) instead of 3. Not a correctness bug -- the two pools are independent with no shared state/ordering between them, no deadlock risk -- but worth tracking alongside the already-tracked per-leg DB-connection-pool footprint finding if usage patterns ever combine to matter at scale. Non-blocking; filed as docs/tasks/backend-data-provider-timeouts-followups-followups.json.

review.notes: Full review: backend suite re-run clean (1491 passed, 100% line/branch coverage, matching the PR's own claim), ruff and mypy (scoped per pyproject.toml's files=["app"], per static-verify) both clean, scripts/check_profit_target_wording.py clean, backend/openapi.json regenerated with zero diff (no route/schema touched, correctly not committed). Dispatched the code-review skill against the diff independently -- returned zero findings after an 8-angle pass including tracing the yfinance 1.7.0 source to confirm .calendar/.info/.insider_transactions touch independent internal cache objects (no shared-mutable-state race across the three concurrent legs). Reproduced the concurrency/mutation-testing claims by hand rather than trusting the self-report, per this task's own instructions: (1) reverted get_extended_data fully to sequential fetches -- test_calendar_info_and_insider_transactions_are_fetched_concurrently correctly failed ('calendar and info did not overlap'); (2) reverted only the fail-fast shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True) to the with-ThreadPoolExecutor(...) (wait=True) form -- test_fast_calendar_failure_returns_promptly_despite_slow_other_properties correctly failed (elapsed ~1.0s vs the <0.5s assertion); (3) removed _clamp_session_timeout's inner post-lock re-check -- test_second_racer_sees_already_clamped_state_after_acquiring_the_lock correctly failed; (4) removed the except Exception: pass around the attribute-assignment step -- test_attribute_assignment_failure_is_a_silent_no_op correctly failed with the AttributeError propagating. All four reverts were restored immediately after each confirmation and the tree verified clean (git diff --stat empty) before moving to the next. This covers both new/hardened tests in the integration suite and the two coverage-closing unit tests in yfinance_provider.py's own test file. All four decisions entries are genuine, specific, and substantive -- not boilerplate. Item 3 (deferring the 4-call-site ThreadPoolExecutor consolidation) and item 5 (reconfirming the DB connection-pool footprint with no code change) are both reasonable, well-argued judgment calls rather than corner-cutting: item 3's rationale correctly distinguishes get_analysis's fail-fast/scoped-session shape from the other three call sites' full-wait shape, and item 5 explicitly considered and rejected two concrete alternatives (explicit pool sizing, a lighter-weight per-leg resource) with reasoning tied to the parent PR's own empirical load test rather than just asserting it's fine. No API/schema surface touched -- openapi.json regeneration correctly produces zero diff. No frontend/UI surface in this PR (a backend data-provider concurrency fix plus tests) -- browser walkthrough (step 9) and the persisted e2e suite (step 9a) both explicitly skipped as not applicable. index.json's state mirror was correct at review time (testing). No stale pr_decision field was present to clear.
